Lindane has been used but is no longer recommended as a first-line treatment due to its neurotoxicity and resist- ance. To be effective insecticide products need to be ap- plied correctly; a quantity of 50 to 100 mL should be ap- plied thoroughly to the hair from hair root to the tip and left on for 8 to 12 hours. Insecticide products kill only adult lice and not the ova, therefore treatment is usually repeated 7 days later. Close contacts should be screened and if in- fected with living lice should also receive treatment. Resistance has been reported to the currently used insecti- cides. Resistance is considered to be most likely to pyre- throids, intermediate to malathion, and least likely to car- baryl. In the UK the policy of rotating insecticides on a district-wide basis in order to overcome the development of resistance is now considered outdated. The current rec- ommendation in the case of suspected resistance and treat- ment failure is to use an insecticide from a different class for the next course. Lotions are preferred to shampoos for head lice since contact time with the insecticide is longer and treatment is thus more effective. A head louse repel- lent containing piperonal is available. Non-insecticide treatments include a 4% dimeticone lotion8 (see p.2032) and wet-combing (also called ‘bug-busting’) with condi- tioner.9 Dimeticone is thought to act by disrupting the abil- ity of the lice to manage their water balance. Dimeticone is applied similarly to the insecticide products and 2 treat- ments are also required to kill any newly hatched nymphs. A dry-on, suffocation-based pediculicide has also been claimed to be effective,10,11 although some have ques- tioned the claims.12 Infestations of crab lice and body lice respond to the same insecticides as head lice. Aqueous solutions are generally preferred to alcoholic for crab louse infestations, since the latter may irritate excoriated skin and genitalia. Malathion has also been suggested for treatment of infes- tation of the eye lashes and brows with pubic lice (pthiria- sis or phthiriasis palpebrarum). Other treatments have in- cluded the application of a thick layer of yellow soft paraffin or application of yellow mercuric oxide 1% eye ointment twice daily for about 7 or 8 days or a single ap- plication of fluorescein eye drops. Body louse infestations in the developed world are mainly seen in homeless individuals, and often respond to the pro- vision of opportunities for simple hygiene.
